title: vuln: the scanned-module list is hardcoded in two places, so a third module is silently unscanned
description:
The set of Go modules to scan is written out literally in two places:
`.github/workflows/vuln.yml`'s change detection paths, and the `vuln` recipe in
the `justfile`. Both name `test/data/codegen` by hand.

A third module added later is therefore both unwatched (the workflow will not
trigger on its dependency changes) and unscanned (the recipe will not visit it)
— silently, with no diagnostic and no failing gate.

That is the same defect class `gqlc-rohp` exists to fix: a required security
gate that is green because it is looking at nothing. rohp closed the instance;
this closes the mechanism that produced it.

Confirmed by the adversarial reviewer at `0475cdb`: the repo currently has
exactly two `go.mod` files and exactly one build tag (`codegen_live`, 4 files),
so there is **no third blind spot today**. This is prophylactic, which is why it
was ruled out of scope for rohp rather than folded in.

Fix: derive the module list rather than declaring it — discover `go.mod` files
under the tree and iterate, in both the recipe and the workflow's path filter.
If the workflow's path filter cannot be made dynamic, then at minimum add a
check that fails when the discovered module set differs from the declared one,
so adding a module forces the lists to be updated rather than silently
bypassing them.

Acceptance: add a third throwaway module with a known-vulnerable dependency and
confirm `just vuln` reports it without anyone editing a path list.

title: codegen/neo4j: positional decoder locals leave index gaps at nullable properties
description:
`gqlc-ak39` replaced neo4j's user-derived decoder locals with positional
generator-owned ones (`value0`, `value1`, …), which closed the whole capture
class rather than special-casing a reserved list.

`valueName(i)` indexes over **all** fields, including nullable ones — but the
nullable arm emits its own block with generator-fixed locals and never consumes
a `value<i>`. So a decoder with interleaved nullable properties emits

    value0, value1, [nullable block], value3, [nullable block], value6, value8…

See `test/data/codegen/valid/entity_property_shadows_decoder_local/golden/neo4j-go-v5/models.go`,
which jumps `value1` → `value3`.

Entirely harmless — the indices are unique by construction, which is the only
property the scheme needs, and Go's unused-variable rule makes any positional
mis-wiring a compile error regardless of density. Purely a legibility point:
the gaps read like something was deleted, and a reader of generated code who
notices will go looking for a bug that is not there.

Fix if anyone touches this code for another reason: increment the counter only
on the required arm, so the emitted sequence is dense `value0..valueN`. Not
worth a standalone change and a full neo4j golden churn (~80 files) on its own.

title: bd-gh-sync: an empty bead description is an unconditional ALLOW, and nothing pins it
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync` decides pull eligibility with a prefix test: GitHub's
body must start with the bead description. When the bead description is the
empty string, `"".startswith("")` — and indeed `anything.startswith("")` — is
universally true, so the bead is unconditionally ALLOWed and GitHub's body is
pulled over it whatever it contains.

Found in the round-3 adversarial review of `fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity` at
`d25d947`.

Ruled out of scope for that branch for a specific reason worth preserving: the
behaviour is **identical under the old subset rule**, so it is not a regression
that branch introduced. It is the degenerate endpoint of a bd-side deletion —
if a description has been emptied on the bd side, there is nothing to protect,
and pulling GitHub's version is arguably the right answer.

What makes it worth a bead is not the behaviour but the absence of a pin. The
sibling case (trailing-block deletion, [[gqlc-6mx3]]) IS covered by a fixture;
this one is not. So nobody would notice if a future change made the empty-desc
path do something else, and this script has now failed review three times for
exactly the reason that its fixture set could not express the input in
question.

Minimum work: add a test asserting the current behaviour, so the decision
becomes deliberate rather than incidental. Then decide separately whether
unconditional ALLOW on an empty description is actually what we want, or
whether an empty description should HOLD on the grounds that it is more likely
to be an accident than an intent.

title: bd-gh-sync: the moved-bead list truncates by id sort, so the interesting id can be the one dropped
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync:267-268` truncates the moved-bead list with `head -n 3`
over an **id-sorted** list, appending `+N more`.

Found in the round-3 adversarial review of `fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity` at
`d25d947`. The reviewer constructed a run with 5 moved beads where the
interesting one sorts last, and got `(m-a, m-b, m-c, +2 more)` — the id of the
bead that actually mattered appears only in output lines that `tail -1`
discards.

Ruled non-blocking and out of scope for that branch because the **count**
survives into the last line, and the count is the actionable trigger: an
operator who sees `+2 more` knows to go look. Nothing is silently lost, only
inconveniently placed.

Worth doing anyway because the ordering is arbitrary — id sort has no relation
to interestingness. Options: sort by recency of change, or drop the truncation
entirely (a moved-bead list is already an exceptional event, so its length is
naturally bounded), or keep the truncation but make the omitted ids reachable
without re-running.

Related: [[bd-gh-sync-tail-1-contract]] — several findings on this script share
the same underlying constraint, that the session-start consumer reads only
`tail -1`, so anything actionable has to be on the last line.

title: bd-gh-sync: no circuit breaker on the ALLOW count
description:
Nothing caps how many beads a single run can hand to --prefer-github. The 129-vs-4 near-miss was caught by eye, not by the script. The ALLOW count does surface in the summary line, but that line prints on total failure too (the fail-open-in-reporting finding, promoted to blocking on gqlc-63y).

Once the eligibility rule narrows to append-only (gqlc-63y), the blast radius drops sharply, which is why this is P3 rather than a blocker there.

PROVENANCE: non-blocking finding 6 in the bd-gh-sync adversarial review (2026-08-01).

FIX: refuse and report when ALLOW exceeds a threshold (or a fraction of the mirrored corpus) rather than proceeding.

title: resolver: two distinct swapped pairs in one candidate set are fixture-uncovered
description:
A candidate set can contain TWO distinct swapped pairs, reachable via a 2x2 endpoint cross-product with all four EdgeKeys declared. The orientation-ambiguity refusal resolves first-in-candidate-order, and that order is deterministic (satisfyingNodeTypes sorts at internal/resolver/resolve.go:1391), so the behaviour is well-defined — but no fixture covers it, so the determinism is unasserted.

PROVENANCE: raised as a non-blocking finding in the gqlc-kph4 adversarial review (2026-08-01). I ruled it out of scope there: kph4 already carries three blockers plus three promoted findings, and this one asserts a property that holds today rather than fixing a defect.

FIX: add an invalid fixture with four declared EdgeKeys over a 2x2 endpoint cross-product; assert the refusal message names a stable pair.

title: vuln: clear the three uncalled advisories the widened scan now surfaces
description:
Widening the scan in gqlc-rohp made the nested module test/data/codegen report three advisories that govulncheck classifies as not-called, so the gate exits 0 and does not block:

- GO-2026-5158 — go.opentelemetry.io/otel v1.41.0, baggage parsing no longer caps raw header length. Imported, not called. Fixed in v1.42.0.
- GO-2026-5841 — github.com/klauspost/compress v1.18.5, OOB read in .../s2. Required, not imported. Fixed in v1.18.7.
- GO-2026-5932 — golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp unmaintained and unsafe by design. Required, not imported. No fix available; nothing in this tree imports openpgp, so this one is permanent noise unless x/crypto drops the package.

Both fixable ones are indirect deps of testcontainers-go v0.43.0. Not bumped in gqlc-rohp because there is no reachable exposure and pinning indirect deps ahead of the module that requires them is churn that go mod tidy can undo. Bump them when testcontainers-go next moves, or pin deliberately if the classification changes to called.

Also worth reporting upstream: govulncheck v1.6.0 silently drops the imports of an in-package test variant, because it keys loaded packages by import path and `p [p.test]` collides with `p`. Reproduced minimally — identical module, identical deps, identical flags, only `package v` vs `package v_test` differing: the in-package form reported nothing, the external form reported the vulnerability with a call trace. gqlc-rohp works around it by keeping the live battery an external test package, held by test-codegen-fence.

title: resolver/codegen: rationale text from the edge-set work is incomplete or reaches across layers
description:
Three comment/citation sites left by gqlc-35yu.9. None change behaviour; each
is a place where the text a future reader is asked to trust says less than the
code guarantees, or justifies itself from the wrong layer.

1. internal/resolver/resolve.go, edgeProbes' doc comment, and
   docs/specs/resolver-stage-r3.md §4.4. Both name `src == tgt` as THE reason
   two probes can name one key. Under ADR 0022 plural endpoints there is a
   second: overlapping srcs/tgts give (A,B) twice with A != B. The
   postcondition (the result is a set) is unaffected — the enumeration dedupes
   on the whole EdgeKey, not on the self-loop condition — but the stated
   rationale is not exhaustive, so a reader checking the code against the
   reason would conclude the dedupe is dead on the plural path. See gqlc-kph4,
   which is the coverage side of the same observation.

2. internal/resolver/resolve_test.go, TestEdgeUnionKeysAreASet. Its comment
   justifies the assertion by what codegen does with a duplicate (emits the
   switch case twice, package fails to compile). AGENTS.md discourages
   cross-layer appeals: the resolver's own reason to return a set is R3 §4.6
   dispatching on the candidate count, which is true whether or not codegen
   exists. Restate it from the resolver's contract and let the codegen
   consequence be at most a closing aside.

3. internal/codegen/prepare.go, admitEdgeUnionCandidates. The first gate (fewer
   than two candidates) cites "R3 spec §4.4" for the invariant it is asserting.
   The third gate — two candidates sharing an edge label — likewise depends on
   the resolver having returned a set rather than a bag, since a bag would
   reach it as a false duplicate-label refusal. It carries no citation. Give it
   the same one.
notes:
MANAGER SEQUENCING NOTE (2026-08-01). Deliberately NOT staffed in parallel with
gqlc-kph4, which is in flight on feat/resolver-plural-undirected-coverage.

This bead's item 1 is the edgeProbes doc comment and R3 spec §4.4 — the exact
text kph4 will be rewriting, because kph4's whole subject is the plural-endpoint
path those two currently describe incompletely. Two agents editing the same
paragraphs concurrently produces a conflict whose resolution is a judgement
call neither of them is placed to make.

Items 2 and 3 (TestEdgeUnionKeysAreASet's cross-layer justification, and the
missing R3 §4.4 citation on admitEdgeUnionCandidates' third gate) are genuinely
independent of kph4 and could have gone now. Kept together with item 1 anyway:
splitting one small comment-accuracy bead into two branches and two PRs costs
more review attention than it saves wall-clock, and item 1 is the one with real
content.

Staff immediately once kph4 lands, and re-read item 1 first — kph4 may have
already made it true, in which case this bead shrinks to items 2 and 3.

title: docs: sentinel taxonomy tables in docs/specs drift from codegen.allSentinels, with no fence
description:
docs/specs/codegen-stage-c3.md, c4.md, c5.md and c6.md carry taxonomy tables mapping
constructs to error sentinels, plus a mirror of codegen.allSentinels annotated with the
stage that introduced each. Nothing checks those tables against the Go slice, so they
drift.

Known drift as of gqlc-35yu.9:
  - the LIST / ANY property refusal added for apache-age-pgx-v5 (round 2) routes
    through ErrUnrepresentableWidth and is not in the construct tables
  - ErrUnrepresentableEdgeUnion (round 3, shared Phase A gate) is in neither the
    construct tables nor the allSentinels mirror

Raised by Carmack during gqlc-35yu.9 and deliberately not fixed there: the branch's own
precedent left the tables alone, and a drive-by two-row edit on an AGE-owned branch is
the wrong unit of work for drift that is already several entries deep.

Do this as one sweep: reconcile every table against allSentinels, and decide whether
the stage specs are historical records of what stage Cn delivered (in which case a
sentinel added by a later epic does not belong in them, and the mirror needs a new home)
or a live index (in which case add a fence that fails when the two disagree, the way
TestSentinelReachability already forces fixture coverage).
notes:
Fence landed on chore/sentinel-taxonomy-fence. Forks resolved:

(1) Historical record vs live index — HISTORICAL, decided on evidence rather than
taste. C2/C3/C4/C5 taxonomy tables name ErrOutOfC2Scope..ErrOutOfC5Scope, sentinels
retired by the per-stage rename; a fence over them would demand falsifying what each
stage shipped. C6 §7 also declares itself the last stage, so a sentinel arriving after
it has no stage spec left to be recorded in — the mirror genuinely has nowhere to go
inside the series. So the stage specs freeze and the mirror gets a new home:
docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md, a live index the fence owns. One pointer line
added to C6 §7 saying the live index moved; C0–C5 untouched, since a reader following
the series arrives at C6 and the new doc explains the relationship.

(2) Fence shape — plain Go test, TestSentinelTaxonomy in internal/codegen/errors_test.go,
inside package codegen so it reads allSentinels directly. No new just recipe and no new
CI job: the required-context list on master is exact, and splitting a job silently
deletes a context. The existing `test` job runs it.

(3) Naming the slice members — the test parses errors.go with go/parser and binds
ident->value through the errors.New message literal, rather than a hand-written
name switch. conformance_test.go sentinelIdent is already such a switch and is a third
mirror of the same set; adding a fourth to fence the second would be the disease. The
fence asserts message uniqueness so the binding stays sound.

(4) Three directions, not two. index<->allSentinels; taxonomy rows<->index; and
declared-in-errors.go <-> documented (index union excluded). The third is the one the
first two cannot see: a sentinel declared and left out of allSentinels leaves both other
sets agreeing on a membership that never grew.

(5) Rejected: asserting document row order matches slice order. Buys tidy diffs, costs a
red suite on a legitimate reorder.

(6) Rejected: naming age.ErrUnsupportedQuery / ErrUnsupportedSchema in the doc. They are
outside allSentinels and have no exported set to fence, so naming them would add exactly
the kind of unfenced claim this bead exists to remove. The preamble says backend packages
carry their own sentinels without naming symbols.

Drift found, all of it fixed on the same branch so the fence lands green:
  - ErrUnrepresentableEdgeUnion is in allSentinels and has two invalid fixtures, and
    appears in zero files under docs/. C6 §7 says fifteen sentinels; the slice has sixteen.
  - ErrUnrepresentableWidth catchment is stale in kind, not just in rows. C3/C4/C5 tables
    enumerate "the eight unrepresentable widths" as a property of the language. Since the
    AGE backend it is the target TypeMap answer: AGE also refuses BYTES, the five
    temporals, LIST and ANY, and unrepresentable_width_list_schema /
    unrepresentable_width_any_schema pin widths no table names. The live doc states the
    backend-relative rule instead of enumerating.
  - The tables carry a stage-relative "Retires at" column that stopped meaning anything at
    C6. The live doc drops it and keeps an "Introduced" column that can hold a bead id.

Verified by mutation, not by assertion: six drift modes each fail with a message naming
the doc, the section and the edit — missing index row (the real drift), index naming a
retired sentinel, missing construct row, missing exclusion row, misspelt sentinel, and a
construct routed to a non-reachable sentinel. Gates: just test, just lint, just
actionlint, just test-codegen-fence all green.
REVIEW: VERDICT FAIL. Manager confirms two of the three blockers by direct test; the third by reading. Returned for a fix round.

The fence itself is sound. The reviewer broke it six ways and it named the document and the section every time; I had already broken it a seventh (an undeclared sentinel) with the same result. Every one of the author's five claims verified. The problem is not the fence — it is what the fence is fencing, and a hole in the one axis the fence was built for.

B1 (BLOCKING). docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md:81 states a phase at which the refusal cannot fire:

  | ErrUnrepresentableWidth | A projected column, or a query parameter, whose property width the target's type table has no carrier for. | Phase A |

Prepare runs phaseZAdmit before phaseAAdmit (prepare.go:238), and phaseZAdmit walks every property of every node and edge type, so any width the target refuses always loses at Phase Z. The code says so itself, in phaseAAdmit's own doc comment (prepare.go:544-547): "Phase Z already caught schema-side offenders so a column projecting an unrepresentable-width property is unreachable unless the query declares an unrepresentable width on a parameter."

I read that comment directly rather than take the report's word. Note it is the COLUMN half of the row that is unreachable; the parameter half is fine. So the row is half-wrong rather than wholly wrong, which is if anything worse — it reads as authoritative and a contributor cannot tell which half to trust. Corroborating: all five unrepresentable_width_* fixtures are *_schema, and §4 step 3 tells a contributor to add a fixture per construct, which for the column half is impossible.

The reviewer flags the same defect at :90 (ErrAliasRequired at Phase B, where prepare.go:717 calls rowFieldName(col.Name) on a column prepare.go:579 already called it on in Phase A — identical predicate, identical input, byte-identical error strings). I have not verified that second instance myself; the implementer should, and should say which way it went.

This is precisely the failure the fence cannot see. A fence holds a document against the code for CONSISTENCY. Nothing holds its prose against the code for CORRECTNESS, so the prose has to be right at commit time. Shipping a wrong phase inside a document whose header calls itself "the live index", in a bead whose entire premise is that documentation drifted from code, is not acceptable.

B2 (BLOCKING). errors_test.go:176-177 has a silent `continue` on the axis the AST parse exists for:

  if !ok || len(value.Names) != 1 || len(value.Values) != 1 { continue }

I reproduced this myself. Adding to errors.go's own var block:

  ErrMultiA, ErrMultiB = errors.New("multi a"), errors.New("multi b")

— two sentinels, one ValueSpec, absent from allSentinels, documented nowhere — leaves `go test -run TestSentinelTaxonomy ./internal/codegen/` GREEN. Direction (c) is bypassed by a comma.

What makes this blocking rather than a gap: twelve lines below, at :184, the author writes a LOUD Require for the adjacent failure mode (declared as something other than errors.New), and it fires correctly. The same author, in the same function, treated one neighbour as a hard error and the other as a skip. That asymmetry is not a scoping decision, and it is one line.

Second bypass of the same axis: errors_test.go:165 parses the single file "errors.go", so a sentinel declared in any other file of package codegen is invisible to (c). parser.ParseDir over the package closes it. Nothing in the repo pins sentinels to errors.go.

B3 (BLOCKING, accepted on the reviewer's evidence). §2 omits the list-leaf construct for ErrUnrepresentableEdgeUnion. admitEdgeUnionCandidates has two call sites (prepare.go:597 column, prepare.go:1013 list-element chain), and invalid/unrepresentable_edge_union_shared_label_list has its own committed fixture for the second. §2's preamble asserts a sentinel carries EVERY construct in its catchment, and §2 does carry list-leaf rows for ErrUnrepresentableWidth and ErrOutOfC6Scope. So the document breaks its own stated contract, on the exact sentinel whose absence from the docs motivated this bead.

NON-BLOCKING, and I am ruling on each rather than leaving them to the implementer:

N1 — §3 is an unaudited silencing valve. The reviewer dropped ErrUnrepresentableEdgeUnion from allSentinels, moved its row to §3 with the text "Silenced by fiat.", deleted both fixtures, and the whole codegen tree stayed green while prepare.go:671 still returns that sentinel. That is real, but it is NOT a regression — the pre-commit state was no better, and the escape needs three coordinated edits. The repo already has the counter-measure in another package (internal/schema/gql/sentinel_coverage_test.go, TestAllSentinelsAreReachable, which reads errors off the wire for exactly this reason). FILE AS A FOLLOW-UP, do not fix here. The bead is about drift between doc and code; reachability is a different axis and deserves its own bead rather than being smuggled into this one.

N2 — three rows present defensive branches (prepare.go:589, :650-655, whose own comments say a synthetic seam is required to reach them) as ordinary user-refusable constructs. FIX HERE. It is the same class as B1 — a contributor will try to write an impossible fixture — and the document already has a section for the distinction.

N3 — ":13 says three renames ago; the chain C2->C3->C4->C5->C6 is four." FIX HERE. It is one word, and the sentence is load-bearing for the design fork the author used to justify the whole approach.

N4 — ":29-30 says allSentinels is the closed set Generate may return on user input", falsified by age.ErrUnsupportedQuery, which is not in allSentinels. FIX HERE, as the reviewer suggests: "the shared front end may return", not "Generate".

N5, N6, N7 — leave. N5 and N6 are diagnosable in seconds, N7 is inherited wording from the repo's own sweepIdentifiers comment and changing it here widens the diff for no gain.
Review FAIL addressed on the same branch.

B1b, the ErrAliasRequired-at-Phase-B question the manager left open: the flag is
CORRECT, the branch is unreachable. Structurally, prepare.go:579 (Phase A) and :717
(Phase B) both call rowFieldName(col.Name) over the same q.Validated.Columns of the
same q, rowFieldName is a pure function of its argument, and Prepare runs phaseAAdmit
to completion before phaseBDerive, first-offender-wins. So Phase A always returns
first, with a byte-identical message.

Rather than argue it, I instrumented all eighteen sentinel fail-sites in prepare.go
with a file-sink counter and ran the whole suite. Only five are reached:
EU_shared_label (x5), A_alias (x4), A_nonproperty_param (x2), L_width (x1),
L_unknown_type (x1). The Phase B alias site is not among them, nor is the Phase A
width-column site. First attempt at this measurement used println and read as
"nothing is reachable" — go test hides passing packages stderr. Worth remembering.

The same sweep corrected two rows the review did not flag, in both directions:
  - the list-leaf width row (L_width) and the list-leaf no-arm row (L_unknown_type)
    ARE reached, so they stay in the reachable table. I had been about to demote the

Document restructured rather than patched: §2 now carries reachable constructs only,
new §3 "Branches no input reaches" carries the six shadowed/defensive branches with

Fence gained a fourth assertion, TestUnreachedBranchesNameRealSentinels: a §3 row
must name a sentinel allSentinels still holds. Six drift modes re-verified against

Gates: just test, just lint, just actionlint, just test-codegen-fence all green.
HANDOFF 2026-08-01. Refix committed at 097cc79 on chore/sentinel-taxonomy-fence, tree clean. Adversarial review of the refix was dispatched and DIED ON SESSION QUOTA before a verdict — NO VERDICT EXISTS, do not merge. Re-dispatch against 097cc79.

Highest-value attacks for the next reviewer: (a) the new section 3 'Branches no input reaches' documents SIX dead branches — for each, is it unreachable by a structural argument (an earlier phase tests a strictly weaker predicate on the same data) or merely un-hit by today's fixtures? A coverage gap filed as documented intent is worse than the original bug; (b) does ANYTHING fail when a section 3 branch becomes reachable again, or does the new fourth assertion only check that the names are real sentinels? (c) is the PHASE column fenced at all, or only the name — if phase is unfenced the entire B1 class returns silently, and B1 was a phase error; (d) re-run the ErrMultiA/ErrMultiB repro then push past it: an explicit-typed var, one built by fmt.Errorf(%w), one assigned from a non-errors.New call, one in a var(...) block mixed with non-error vars, one in a build-tagged file, an Err-named non-error, and an error not named Err — every silent skip is B2 again in a new coat.

title: codegen: narrow-width property conversions wrap silently instead of erroring
description:
A property whose schema width is narrower than the carrier the driver hands back is
converted at the field with a plain Go conversion, so a value that does not fit wraps
silently rather than failing. Found by Linus during review of gqlc-35yu.9.

Pre-existing and cross-backend: AGE narrows agtype's int64/float64 carriers to the
declared INT32/UINT64/FLOAT32 width, and the neo4j targets do the same from their own
carriers. Neither reports the loss.

This is a correctness question, not a codegen-mechanics one: a store can hold a value
outside the declared width (nothing in AGE or neo4j enforces a GQL property type at
write time unless the writer went through gqlc), so the read path is where it surfaces.

Decide the posture before implementing. Options: range-check at the field and fail the
decode; range-check and saturate; document that the schema's declared width is trusted.
Whichever is chosen must be the same on every backend, since the emitted surface is
backend-invariant, and it needs corpus coverage at the boundary values.

title: codegen/age: a multi-label node or edge type refuses the whole schema
description:
age.rejectMultiLabelSchema fails generation when the schema declares a node or
edge type keyed on more than one label. Verified against apache/age 1.7.0:
`CREATE (x:A:B {n: 1})` is a syntax error — AGE stamps exactly one label on a
vertex or an edge and its parser has no syntax for a second — so a graph
matching such a type cannot be written through this backend and no value
matching it can arrive to be decoded.

The gate is on the schema's whole entity table rather than on the columns a
batch projects, because Phase Z names an entity for every type in the schema
and the emitted Go surface is backend-invariant: a struct no query could fill
is still a struct the package would have to declare, with a label check
nothing could satisfy.

The cost is the same shape as gqlc-35yu.13's: a schema carrying one multi-label
type refuses AGE generation for the whole batch, including queries that never
touch it. test/data/codegen/valid/entity_multi_label_named is the fixture; it
is enrolled for neo4j-go-v5 only.
acceptance_criteria:
Either:
- a per-entity admission lands in the shared prepare phase, so a backend can
  refuse one entity without refusing the schema, and the AGE gate narrows to
  the queries that actually project the refused type; or
- the bead closes recording that whole-schema refusal is the right posture,
  with the reason stated where an author hitting it will find it.

title: codegen/age: fence that every AGE target emits an identical SessionInit
description:
All 12 apache-age-pgx-v5 golden targets carry their own copy of SessionInit.
Nothing asserts directly that the copies agree.

Today they agree by construction -- SessionInit is emitted from one template
with no per-target variation -- and the codegen fence proves each golden
matches what the emitter produces. So the property holds transitively. What
is unpinned is the template gaining a per-target conditional: the fence would
stay green while the copies diverged.

This matters because live_age_session_test.go binds ONE package's SessionInit
to pools that hand out handles generated into others. That binding is only
sound while the copies issue the same statements. The live arm checks the two
packages it mixes (rightly -- that is its own precondition), but the general
claim is a pure-text property of the emitted tree and does not belong behind a
testcontainer.

Assert it offline: read SessionInit's body out of every
test/data/codegen/valid/*/golden/apache-age-pgx-v5/graph.go and require all 12
byte-identical. No container, runs in the default build, fails the moment the
template grows a per-target branch.

Found by Linus as NB2 on gqlc-35yu.8, where the finding was ruled a naming
defect in that bead's own test and the exhaustive claim was split out to here.

title: codegen: dollarTag is computed on bytes the emitted raw string does not carry
description:
Both backends emit a query's text as a Go RAW string literal:

    internal/codegen/age/render_queries.go:89
    internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go:179
    fmt.Fprintf(&b, "const %sQueryText = `%s`\n\n", p.Bare, p.SourceText)

Those two lines are byte-identical, so this is epic-wide, not an AGE gap.

## The invariant that breaks

Go discards carriage returns inside raw string literals -- it is in the spec,
not an implementation detail. So the VALUE of the emitted constant is
p.SourceText with every \r removed, while everything computed at generate time
was computed on p.SourceText WITH them. I checked internal/queryfile for
normalisation and found none, so a CRLF-authored .cypher file carries \r into
SourceText and the two byte strings genuinely differ.

For neo4j the consequence is cosmetic: \r\n and \n are the same query to the
server.

For AGE it is not, because dollarTag (age/render_queries.go:52) chooses the
dollar-quote delimiter by scanning the text, and gqlc-35yu.7 established that
the delimiter must be chosen against exactly the bytes the parser will scan --
that was B1, where a tag occurrence straddling the text/tag boundary produced
generated code that could not run. This is the same invariant failing for a
different reason: dollarTag scans the pre-emission bytes, and the parser sees
the post-emission ones. Removing \r can create a $gqlc-shaped occurrence that
dollarTag never saw.

## Reachability is narrow -- confirm before investing

Ordinary CRLF puts \r at line ends, which cannot forge $gqlc$: a trailing
`$gqlc\r\n` still has \n after the token, not $. Breaking it needs a bare \r
INSIDE the token, e.g. `$gql\rc` at the very end of the text, which no normal
authoring produces. That is why the .7 reviewer filed it non-blocking and why I
did not hold the merge for it.

Do NOT start by writing the fix. Start by deciding whether the reachable set is
empty. If it is, the right change may just be to normalise line endings at
queryfile read time so generate-time and emission-time bytes are the same by
construction, which kills the class rather than the instance -- and which is
probably worth doing anyway for golden stability across checkouts with
different autocrlf settings.

## Whichever way it goes, leave a fence

.7's TestDollarTagClosesOnlyAtTheEnds (age/render_queries_test.go) covers the
predicate but feeds it strings directly, so it cannot see this: the gap is
between what dollarTag is HANDED and what is EMITTED. A fence has to compare
the emitted constant's value against the bytes the tag was chosen on.

title: codegen tests: sweep the type-map tables against their domain, not a hand-counted length
description:
internal/codegen/age/types_test.go and internal/codegen/neo4j/types_test.go (:45, :60, :96, :118, :155) drive their type-map assertions from hand-written literal tables. Both carried require.Len(table, <literal count>) assertions, which assert that a literal sitting directly above has the length someone counted by hand: they fire only if an editor changes the table and forgets the number, and when they fire they name nothing about what was lost. The AGE ones were removed in gqlc-35yu.6; the neo4j ones remain.

Removing them leaves a real gap: deleting a row from a table now fails nothing, so a type silently stops being tested.

Fix: assert domain COVERAGE, not length — the union of the representable and unrepresentable tables must ElementsMatch the full domain, the way TestRunDriverAxis sweeps config.DriverValues(). That bites on both growth and shrink and is not tautological, because the expected side is derived rather than counted.

Blocker: the enumerators do not exist. There is no graph.PropertyTypeValues(), no resolver.TemporalValues(), no resolver.ScalarValues() — config.DriverValues() exists only because the YAML loader needed one. This bead adds them to internal/graph and internal/resolver and then sweeps both backends. Note graph.PropertyType is an OPEN string type, so its enumerator is a maintained list rather than a closed set, and the enumerator itself needs a fence.

Do both backends in one change: fixing one leaves the same hole plus an inconsistency.

Out of scope: typeMap.Temporal returning "any" for every kind with no rejection channel is gqlc-9n6t. Temporal has no switch at all, so it has neither growth nor shrink coverage today — but that fence and 9n6t's rejection channel are the same edit, so 9n6t owns it.

title: spec: the :many empty-result contract (empty slice, not nil) is emitted but unspecified
description:
Generated `:many` methods emit `out := make([]RowT, 0, len(records))`, so an empty result set returns a non-nil zero-length slice rather than nil. That is a deliberate emitter choice, but `docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md` never states it — the only nearby line is §'Columns is a non-empty slice', which is about something else.

gqlc-35yu.4 strengthened the live battery from `require.Empty` (which accepts nil) to `require.NotNil`, so the behaviour is now pinned by a test while remaining absent from the spec. Test and spec disagree about what is normative.

Worth settling before gqlc-35yu.8 brings the AGE arm into the same battery: if AGE's emitter reaches for `var out []RowT` the arm fails, and whether that failure is a bug in AGE or an over-tight test is currently unanswerable from the documents. The uniform-generated-interface promise argues for making it normative rather than relaxing the test.
acceptance_criteria: codegen-stage-c1.md states the :many empty-result contract explicitly and distinguishes it from :one's ErrNoRows; the live battery's assertion cites it.

title: codegen tests: narrow-width list-element fixture (int32/float32 in a list) — golden-uncovered conversion branch
description:
Found by adversarial review of gqlc-35yu.1 (2026-07-31), deliberately deferred out of that bead.

No fixture exercises a NARROW-WIDTH LIST ELEMENT (int32 or float32 inside a list), so the driver-carrier conversion branch at internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go:654 is not covered by any golden.

Why it was deferred rather than fixed in gqlc-35yu.1: that bead is a pure refactor whose entire gate is "existing golden trees byte-identical". Adding a fixture there would have introduced NEW golden files into a diff whose whole point is that goldens did not move, muddying the one signal the gate exists to produce.

Why it still matters: gqlc-35yu.1 justified deleting ListElem.Carrier / ListElem.UsesConvert and recomputing them via driverCarrier(e.GoType) on the grounds that the derivation is total. Review confirmed that by substitution over master's code — but for THIS branch specifically, "the goldens prove it" is weaker than it sounds, because no golden reaches it. The substitution argument stands; the empirical backstop does not exist yet.

Add a fixture (suggested name: list_int32) under test/data/codegen/valid with a query projecting a list of a narrow-width numeric type, plus its golden subtree. Note that gqlc-35yu.3 restructures fixtures into one dir with per-target golden subtrees — if that has landed by the time this is picked up, follow the new layout and the manifest targets list rather than the old one.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture exercising a narrow-width list element exists under test/data/codegen/valid with its golden subtree; the conversion branch in the neo4j render path is exercised by the golden suite rather than only by substitution argument.

title: TCK conformance ledger: execute the openCypher TCK against neo4j + AGE and track per-backend coverage
description:
Owner idea, 2026-07-31. Not yet scoped — this bead exists to hold the idea and the design tension, not to authorise a harness.

Proposal: run the whole vendored openCypher TCK generically against BOTH backends (neo4j and Apache AGE), analyse coverage, and incrementally drive it up.

CURRENT STATE
- The TCK is vendored at test/data/query/cypher/tck (tag 2024.3, via `just fetch-tck`).
- It is consumed PARSE-ONLY, by internal/query/cypher/acceptance_test.go, over a SUBSET of feature dirs (match, return, match-where, return-skip-limit, union, with, with-where, return-orderby, with-orderBy, with-skip-limit). Nothing executes TCK scenarios against a live backend.
- gqlc-35yu.4/.8 build a shared live scenario battery with per-backend adapters against live containers. That harness is the natural substrate for this work, which is why this bead depends on the epic.

THE DESIGN TENSION — RESOLVE BEFORE BUILDING
gqlc is a code generator, not a query engine. The TCK tests ENGINE semantics. So "TCK coverage" is ambiguous across three quite different levels, with very different cost and value:
  L1 PARSE      — does gqlc parse the scenario's query? (partially covered today)
  L2 GENERATE   — can gqlc emit code for it? Most TCK scenarios carry no schema and no typed params, so this needs a synthesised schema per scenario.
  L3 EXECUTE    — does the GENERATED code, run against backend X, produce the TCK's expected result table? This is the real prize and by far the most expensive: each scenario ships its own graph fixture as Cypher plus an expected-results table, so the harness must set up, generate, compile, run, and compare.

"100% coverage" is probably the WRONG TARGET. A large fraction of the TCK is out of scope for gqlc BY DESIGN — dynamic queries, and everything gqlc deliberately rejects (C6 scope limits, alias-required expressions, and similar). Chasing 100% would mean either weakening those rejections or permanently carrying a pile of unexplained failures.

The more valuable and actually achievable goal: a CLASSIFIED COVERAGE LEDGER in which every TCK scenario is either passing on a given backend or carries a recorded, reviewed reason for not being — out-of-scope-by-design, backend dialect gap, or genuine gqlc gap. Then the number to drive to zero is "genuine gqlc gaps", not "non-passing scenarios", and the ledger doubles as a per-backend dialect-gap map (which is adjacent to gqlc-35yu.12).

OPEN QUESTIONS
- Which level (L1/L2/L3) is the target? L3 per-backend is what "validate against both implementations" implies, but it is a large harness.
- Is the ledger a committed artefact (reviewable diff when coverage shifts) or a generated report?
- Where does it run? L3 against two live containers is nightly-job shaped, not PR-CI shaped.
acceptance_criteria: Framing agreed with the owner (which of the three coverage levels this targets, and how deliberately-out-of-scope scenarios are classified) before any harness work starts.
notes:
=== FRAMING RESOLVED 2026-08-01 — acceptance criterion met, harness work authorised ===
Decided under standing delegated authority (owner directive 2026-08-01: decide, record,
report). Reversible: nothing is built yet.

1. LEVEL — staged L1 -> L2 -> L3, one ledger spanning all three.
   The three levels are not alternatives; they are columns. A scenario that does not
   parse cannot generate, and one that does not generate cannot execute, so the ledger
   carries a per-level status and the levels gate each other naturally.
   L1 (parse) is backend-INDEPENDENT — it tests gqlc's Cypher front end, not a backend.
   It needs no container and no part of the 35yu epic, so it is separable and starts
   first. Split out as its own bead (see below); gqlc-modl retains L2/L3.
   L3 is the real prize and stays gated on 35yu.4/.8's live harness.

2. "100% COVERAGE" IS THE WRONG TARGET — this reverses the shape of the owner's original
   ask deliberately. A large fraction of the TCK exercises dynamic queries and constructs
   gqlc rejects BY DESIGN (C6 scope limits, alias-required expressions). Driving
   non-passing to zero would mean weakening those rejections. The number driven to zero
   is GENUINE GQLC GAPS.

3. CLASSIFICATION IS A CLOSED ENUM, and unclassified is a hard failure:
     pass | out-of-scope-by-design (must cite the ADR or spec clause) |
     dialect-gap (backend cannot; gqlc could) | gqlc-gap (genuine)
   A scenario present in the vendored TCK with no ledger row, or a row with no reason on
   a non-pass, fails the build. Per AGENTS.md "make illegal states unrepresentable": an
   unexplained failure must not be representable, because that is precisely how a ledger
   decays into a pile of ignored red.

4. THE LEDGER IS A COMMITTED ARTEFACT, not a generated report.
   Why: the value is the reviewable DIFF when coverage shifts. A generated report shows
   state; a committed ledger makes a silent regression — a scenario that stops parsing —
   a red line in a PR diff a human must approve. Direct precedent in this repo: the godog
   skiplist and the mustReject pins are committed for exactly this reason, and AGENTS.md
   already requires skiplist updates to travel in the same branch as the behaviour change
   that causes them. The ledger inherits that rule.

5. WHERE IT RUNS — L1 and L2 in PR CI (pure parse/generate, no containers, no meaningful
   wall-time). L3 in the nightly codegen_live job alongside 35yu.8. PR CI wall-time stays
   untouched, consistent with the epic's locked constraint.

6. SEQUENCING — L1 does not depend on the 35yu epic and may start whenever; L2/L3 stay
   blocked on 35yu.4/.8. gqlc-modl is NOT to be started while the 35yu epic is in flight.

=== CORRECTION 2026-08-01 — the CURRENT STATE above is STALE, and L1 IS ALREADY DONE ===
Read the code before acting on this bead; the description was written from a stale
snapshot. Measured on master at 536931a:

  - internal/query/cypher/acceptance_test.go enrols ALL 37 TCK feature leaf dirs, not the
    10-dir subset the description claims. 220 .feature files, 1615 scenarios.
  - The skiplist carries 140 entries, every one classified into one of EIGHT declared
    skipCategory constants (catRuntimeError, catResultAssertionOnly, catValueBelowBoundary,
    catGroupingKeySemantic, catBindingKindConflict, catWriteShapeConstraint,
    catClauseComposition, catSignatureArgCheck).
  - TestSkiplistCategoryPolicy already enforces both halves of the invariant I specified
    in the framing note: an entry with no valid category fails, AND a declared category
    with zero entries fails as a dead policy slot.
  - The corpus is never edited; skipped scenarios are reported and counted, never deleted.

CONSEQUENCE 1 — do NOT file or build an "L1 ledger" bead. L1 coverage is complete and the
classified-ledger mechanism already exists, in production, with its own policy test. My
framing note above independently specified this design; the repo got there first. That is
a strong signal the pattern is right.

CONSEQUENCE 2 — this bead's job is narrower and cheaper than the description implies:
EXTEND the existing skiplist/skipCategory mechanism to L2 (generate) and L3 (execute per
backend), rather than designing a new ledger format. Same committed-artefact rule, same
"uncategorised is a build failure" rule, same "never delete from the corpus" rule. Reuse
skipCategory's shape; the L3 taxonomy needs at least one new family the L1 set lacks —
backend dialect gap — which is where this bead meets gqlc-35yu.12.

CONSEQUENCE 3 — the honest headline number today is L1 = 1615 scenarios enrolled, 140
deliberately accepted with a recorded policy reason, 0 unexplained. That is the format the
L2/L3 columns should report in.

title: codegen/age: dialect-gap posture for neo4j-only Cypher in user query text
description: User query text executes verbatim (ADR 0005), so a query calling neo4j-only functions (datetime(), duration(), point(), etc.) or unsupported openCypher constructs generates fine for the AGE target and fails at RUNTIME with an AGE error. Decide and implement the posture: document-only (list known gaps, let runtime errors surface them) vs a backend-specific admission hook in shared phase A that flags known-unsupported constructs at generate time. Evidence from the live battery and early AGE usage should inform which gaps are actually hit before building detection machinery. Post-epic backlog: intentionally unblocked, not on the epic critical path.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded (document-only or admission hook) with rationale; if document-only, the generated package or docs name the known gaps; if admission hook, at least the verified-unsupported construct list errors at generate time with invalid fixtures.
notes: SEQUENCING (2026-08-01): deliberately NOT parallelised, despite having no dependency edges. The empty DEPENDS ON is there so this bead cannot block the critical path, not an invitation to start it early — the description asks for evidence from the live battery and early AGE usage before choosing between document-only and an admission hook, and that evidence does not exist until .8 through .11 have run. Starting now would mean deciding the posture blind and then discovering the real gap list afterwards. Scheduled last in the epic, after .11.

title: schema/gql: labelSets' defensive clone is unpinned — dropping it aliases the caller's label slice and the suite stays green
description:
`labelSets` (internal/schema/gql/resolve.go:140-150) builds a declaration's complete
label set by appending the implied labels to the key ones:

    return keyKey, append(slices.Clone(key), implied...).Key(), true

Dropping the clone — `append(key, implied...)` — leaves the entire suite green:

    go build ./...            ok
    go test ./internal/...    ok

That is an unpinned aliasing guard, not an unnecessary one. `append` on a slice with
spare capacity writes into the caller's backing array, so without the clone
labelSets would scribble the implied labels over whatever follows the key labels in
the caller's storage. The caller is resolve()'s node and edge loops, and the slice
is the rawNode/rawEdge's keyLabels — live data that is read again later in the same
pass (resolve.go:57 nodeKeyLabels, :113 edgeKeyLabels).

WHY IT CANNOT BITE TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS NOT REASSURING. Every LabelSet that
reaches labelSets is produced by labelSet() at nodetype.go:36-53, which returns
either `graph.LabelSet{name.GetText()}` (len == cap == 1) or
`make(graph.LabelSet, len(names))` (len == cap). With no spare capacity, append
always reallocates and the clone is redundant. So the clone's correctness depends
on a capacity invariant that

  - is established in a different file from the code that relies on it,
  - is stated nowhere, in a comment or a test, and
  - would be silently undone by any future collector that accumulates labels with
    append rather than sizing a make() up front — which is the obvious way to write
    one, and is how impliedLabels is already threaded through rawNode/rawEdge.

FOUND BY the 29-case mutation sweep of resolve.go (2026-07-28). The file is
otherwise in good shape: 26 of 29 mutations were caught outright, including every
sentinel swap and both duplicate-type checks. This was the only survivor that
represents a real guard. The two others are provably dead writes, recorded in bd
memory and deliberately not filed:

  :61  `if n.alias != ""` gating idx.aliases[n.alias]
  :64  `if n.name != ""` gating idx.declared[n.name]

Both widen to write under the "" key, and neither map is ever read with an empty
key: the only two read sites, resolve.go:209 and :211, sit lexically inside
`if ref.alias != ""` in rawEndpoint.resolve. Equivalent mutants.

THE FIX is a unit test rather than a code change, because the code is already
correct — what is missing is the assertion that keeps it correct.
TestLabelSetsDoesNotWriteThroughItsInput hands labelSets a key slice with spare
capacity and asserts the byte beyond len is untouched. It has to assert on the
backing array rather than on the slice: appending past len leaves the caller's
slice header alone, so `key` reads as one element with or without the clone, and
only the sentinel behind it moves. Verified 1:1 — the test fails with the clone
dropped and passes with it restored, and no other test in the suite moves either
way.
close_reason: Closed

title: test(resolver): pin the group-zero contract stated by three guards in scope.go
description:
The 120-case mutation sweep of internal/resolver/scope.go found three guards
that each state the same contract — group id 0 means "not in an OPTIONAL
group", not "in the group numbered zero" — and no test anywhere pinned any of
them.

    scope.go:403  addMember's    `if v == "" || g <= 0`
    scope.go:427  demoteGroup's  `if g == 0 || demotedGroups[g]`
    scope.go:837  Export's       `if g > 0`

## Why the sweep could not tell them apart

Each survives alone, so on a first read all three look inert. They are not: the
first two mask each other exactly. addMember refuses to enter a group-0 name in
the membership table, and demoteGroup refuses to demote group 0 even if a name
got in. Drop either alone and the other still blocks the cascade. Only the
COMBINED mutation discriminates — with both dropped, a proven non-nullable
binding demotes "group 0", which sweeps up every other groupless name in the
Part.

This is the class-5 mutually-masking pair from the survivor triage, measured
rather than argued:

    SURVIVED   addMember g<=0 alone
    SURVIVED   demoteGroup g==0 alone
    CAUGHT     PAIR addMember + demoteGroup
    CAUGHT     Export g>0 alone

Export's `g > 0` is the third statement of the same contract and a chained
link: relaxed, it writes a zero id into the carry, where addMember rejects it on
arrival. It is only reachable as a defect if addMember is also relaxed, so it
needs its own direct assertion rather than a behavioural one.

## Parser reachability

cypher/listener.go:159-162 records the invariant nullable <=> optionalGroup >= 1,
and build.go:280-290 reaches the nullable constructors only when
optionalGroup > 0, so the violating shape is parser-unreachable today. The
test-only constructor query.NewNullableNodeBinding (query.go:332, no group
argument) can express it at the scope layer, which is where the three guards
live. Same posture as the shadow-cascade tests merged in #569: pin the
invariant where it is stated, and treat parser-reachability as a separate
question.

## Fixed here

internal/resolver/scope_test.go only; no production change.
TestScopeGroupZeroIsNotAnOptionalGroup drives one nullable groupless binding
and one required groupless binding through SeedLocalNullability +
DemoteNullability, asserts the nullable one is not demoted by the other's
witness, and asserts directly that neither name reaches exportedOptionalGroup.

Verified 1:1 — the pair mutation and Export's half are each caught by this test
and by nothing else.

Related: gqlc-bef item 1.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: scope.go sweep residue — 8 of 10 survivors triaged and closed, the last 2 blocked on gqlc-ka1's ADR
description:
The residue of the 120-case mutation sweep of internal/resolver/scope.go that gqlc-efe did not fix. Filed so the next sweep of this file does not re-derive the triage from scratch, and so the genuinely-open items are not lost among the equivalent mutants.

STATUS: eight of the ten items are now closed. The two that remain (3 and 4) are
both blocked on the same ADR — gqlc-ka1's choice between per-fixture message
assertions and split sentinels. Nothing further in this bead is actionable
without that decision.

## Argued inert — do not re-file

  :606  virtualProjection's Hops() TypeList/TypeEdge stamp. Already gqlc-2y7's dead code.
  :298  InferUnlabelled's r3EdgeAdmissible re-check. The code comment says the check already ran at BindEdge, so every edge reaching here has passed it.
  :677  refProjectionType's carried-alias `ref.Property == ""` half. The doc comment says a property lookup on a carried alias is parser-unreachable — the scope check rejects Ref{"c","p"} unless c is a binding name.
  :387  DemoteNullability's 5xg EdgeBinding arm. The comment says it outright: an edge is never bare, so the parser passes a constant false (cypher/pattern.go:314).
  :380, :406, :432  the three "is the name already in the table" present-guards. Dropping them writes false where the entry was absent, and false is also the zero value every reader gets from a missing key, so the mutants are equivalent.
  :583  materialiseReturns' empty-scopeOrder bail. Returns nil rather than an empty non-nil slice; len is 0 either way and nothing compares against nil.
  :481  the endpoint loop's `v == ""`. Unreachable: NewVarEndpoint rejects the empty variable (query.go:1158-1161), and an unnamed endpoint is an InlineEndpoint, a different sum member. Only the zero value VarEndpoint{} could carry "", and no constructor produces one. (Resolved by gqlc-dg3.)
  :759  Export's localGroup `v == ""`. A dead write: localGroup is read at :836 only for names in exportedNames, and buildScopeOrder excludes "" at :540. (Resolved by gqlc-dg3.)
  :486  DemoteNullability's `changed = true` after the node write. Provably redundant rather than untested: nothing reads nullableBinding to decide edge admissibility, so any state change that could enable a new edge also sets changed via demoteGroupsOf at :488. Equivalent mutant.
  :292, :303  InferUnlabelled's two pending gates. See item 7 below.
  :540  buildScopeOrder's `seen[v]` dedup. See item 8 below.
  :232  BindCall's slot nullable bit. Dead field, not a missing test — see item 5 below; it belongs to gqlc-2y7.
  :977-980  WitnessUse's ExprUse error propagation. Unreachable by construction — see item 10 below.

## Closed

1. ~~The group-zero triple~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-nu2 (PR #572). The premise in the original filing was wrong: the three do not all survive together. addMember's `g <= 0` (:403) and demoteGroup's `g == 0` (:427) are a mutually-masking pair (each survives alone, the PAIR is caught), and Export's `g > 0` (:837) is a chained link, inert behind addMember's rejection of a zero id on arrival, so it needs a direct assertion. The answer to "can a binding be Nullable() with OptionalGroup() == 0" is: not from the parser (cypher/listener.go:159-162 records nullable <=> optionalGroup >= 1), but the test-only nullable constructors can express it at the scope layer, which is where the guards live.

2. ~~The anonymous-binding guards~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-dg3 (PR #574), and one of them was a real defect. "Does anything read the "" key" has different answers per site, so they do not triage as a class. Only an EdgeBinding may be anonymous (query.go:86), so two anonymous edges in one Part both write nullableBinding[""] and the last wins — making SeedLocalNullability's :340 and addMember's :403 a load-bearing masking pair that, dropped together, reports OPTIONAL-matched bindings as non-nullable. The other two (:481, :759) moved to the inert list above. See bd memory sweep-shared-sentinel-key-collision.

5. ~~BindCall's slot nullable bit (:232)~~ — CLOSED, and the premise was wrong twice over. The filing said "no fixture yields a nullable CALL YIELD scalar"; valid/call_standalone_yield_star_string_nullable.cypher does exactly that and its golden pins `"nullable": true`. The real reason the bit is unpinned is that it is never read: hard-wiring it to false SURVIVES, and hard-wiring it to true ALSO SURVIVES. Projection nullability comes from a different lane — callProjectionType (resolve.go:719-722) reads `nullableBinding[ref.Variable]`, not `slot.nullable`. Proven by deletion rather than by grep: removing the field from callBindingSlot and its write at :232 leaves `go build ./...`, `go vet` and the full `go test ./internal/...` all green. This is dead code, not a test gap, and gqlc-2y7's 13:36 comment already owns the field family. Moved there; do not re-file here.

6. ~~CloseEdges' deferred-close error (:275-277)~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-0ul (PR #576). Such an input does exist: an edge deferred for an unlabelled endpoint that still fails closure after inference, reached via orientation rather than labels. All six pre-existing negative fixtures spell both endpoints, so none ever defers.

7. ~~InferUnlabelled's two pending gates~~ — CLOSED as inert, measured. Widening `len(bb.Labels()) == 0` (:292) to admit every node SURVIVES, and so does dropping `len(pending) == 0` (:303) and its duplicate at resolve.go:570. The reason :292 does not matter is that inferUnlabelled filters the candidates again at resolve.go:582 (`if len(resolved) > 0`), and THAT filter is pinned — dropping it is CAUGHT by valid/carry_wins_over_unlabelled_rebind.cypher. The two empty-pending bails are pure short-circuits standing immediately ahead of `for len(pending) > 0` (resolve.go:592), which is already a no-op on an empty slice. Equivalent mutants.

8. ~~buildScopeOrder's `seen[v]` dedup (:540)~~ — CLOSED as an equivalent mutant; the premise is impossible, not merely untested. The filing asked for "a Part whose bindings name the same variable twice". No such Part can exist: cypher/pattern.go:398-425's mergeBinding keys on `part.byVar[variable]` and folds a re-reference into the existing binding record, so Part.Bindings is variable-unique by construction. Probed directly — `MATCH (a:Person), (a:Person)`, `MATCH (a:Person) MATCH (a)` and `(p)-[r:KNOWS]->(p)` each yield exactly one binding per variable. A fixture was written for this, measured as non-pinning, and deleted rather than shipped. Agrees with gqlc-2y7's independent TRIPWIRE-S result.

10. ~~WitnessUse's ExprUse error propagation (:977-980)~~ — CLOSED as a defensive tripwire, unreachable by construction. Swallowing the error SURVIVES. resolveType (resolve.go:762-810) returns a non-nil error from exactly two arms: list-of-nodes (:791) and list-of-edges (:793); every other arm returns a value or panics. So the propagation fires only if an ExprUse's EnclosingType is LIST<NODE> or LIST<EDGE> — and it cannot be, because of the thing that creates the ExprUse in the first place. An ExprUse exists only because a parameter sits inside the enclosing expression; a parameter types as TypeUnknown; and listLiteralType (cypher/typing.go:558-568) takes commonType over the elements, which collapses to TypeUnknown the moment two element types differ. So any list containing a parameter has element TypeUnknown. The only other producer of LIST<EDGE>, refType at cypher/expr.go:294, fires on a bare var-length Ref, which is a RefProjection and bypasses resolveType entirely (gqlc-2y7 §2). Probed 22 shapes — list literals, nested lists, concatenation, IN, CASE, coalesce, indexing, SET value, both node and edge — and not one produced a list-of-nodes/edges enclosing type. The two list arms ARE pinned, via the projection path, by invalid/list_of_nodes_projection.cypher and invalid/list_of_edges_projection.cypher.

## Genuinely open — both blocked on gqlc-ka1's ADR

3. PropertyUseWitness's out-of-scope arm (:929-931) is unreachable because WitnessUse gates on Contains() first (:963). Confirmed independently by the gqlc-9gz emitter audit. A guard chain of the listener.go :67 -> :92 -> :113 kind: relax the gate and the downstream arm starts mattering, with no test on it. See bd memory listener-sweep-survivors.

4. refProjectionType's out-of-scope arm (:680) — DIAGNOSED by gqlc-9gz (PR #578), still open to fix. The full ErrOutOfR0Scope audit found eighteen emitters against five fixtures, with the five mapping 1:1 onto the five proven sites. :680 is unreached because resolve.go:200 rejects path/unwind bindings first; relax :200 and :680 covers for it, raising the identical sentinel from another file. Pinning :680 on its own therefore needs either a per-fixture message assertion or a split sentinel — that is gqlc-ka1's ADR, so it was deliberately not done. The ten defensive emitters are enumerated in gqlc-9gz and should not be re-filed.

## Method note

Two of the three items closed first were mutually-masking pairs whose members each read as inert alone. The COMBINED mutation is what discriminates, and it should be run on any group of guards that state the same contract *before* concluding they are equivalent.

More generally: in six of the eight closed items the original filing's stated premise turned out to be wrong or incomplete — not the verdict, the *reason*. Item 5 was filed as "no fixture covers this" when a fixture does cover it and the field is simply unread. Item 8 asked for an input the parser cannot construct. Item 1 asserted the three guards survive together when the middle pair does not. Measure the premise, do not argue it; and when a mutation survives, find out *which* downstream site is covering for it before deciding what the survival means.

## Sentinel-coverage note (from gqlc-9gz)

Per-sentinel coverage is not per-emitter coverage. ErrOutOfR0Scope had five
fixtures and eighteen emitters, and TestSentinelReachability was green
throughout. Worse, a fixture can prove a sentinel reachable without proving
*which site* raises it: if removing the guard under test leaves the query
failing with the same sentinel from a downstream site, the mutation survives.
Write the fixture so that removing the guard makes it PASS. See bd memory
sweep-negative-fixture-must-not-name-rejected-binding.

## Two ways a survivor can be "covered for" (generalised from items 7 and 10)

Both closed-as-inert items this round were survivors whose contract was held up
somewhere else, and the two mechanisms are worth naming because they look
identical from the sweep output:

  - A LATER FILTER restates the guard. :292 admits too much, but resolve.go:582
    narrows it again before anything observes the difference. The later filter is
    the one worth pinning; the earlier one is an optimisation.
  - THE INPUT CANNOT BE BUILT. :977-980 needs an ExprUse over a list of nodes,
    and the parameter that creates the ExprUse is exactly what forces the list's
    element type to UNKNOWN. The guard is not untested, it is unreachable, and
    the proof lives in the producer (typing.go's commonType), not in the consumer.

The first deserves a test somewhere else in the chain. The second deserves a
comment in situ and nothing more.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: canonicalSpelling's comma-space collapse is dead code until gqlc-5md lands, and nothing pins it
description:
Found by a 31-case mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go (24/31 caught). Both comma-collapsing lines in collapseParenthetical can be deleted with the full suite green:

    propertytype.go:289    inner = strings.ReplaceAll(inner, " ,", ",")
    propertytype.go:290    inner = strings.ReplaceAll(inner, ", ", ",")

## This is not a missing fixture

The obvious diagnosis — nothing feeds a comma-bearing spelling through — is wrong, and checking it first is what makes the rest of this bead worth writing. The suite already drives all four comma-bearing grammar arms end to end:

  - propertytype_test.go:239   FLOAT(10, 2)
  - propertytype_test.go:244   DECIMAL(10, 2)
  - propertytype_test.go:273   DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL
  - corpus_area_d1_test.go:267 STRING(2, 5)
  - corpus_area_d1_test.go:291 BYTES(1, 10)

They exercise the lines and still cannot observe them.

## Why — provable for every input, not just the ones in the suite

canonicalSpelling's result is consumed at exactly two sites, both in normaliseType:

  :253   typeSpellings[full]
  :256   typeSpellings[truncateParenthetical(full)]

At :253, no key in typeSpellings contains a comma (every parenthesised row is a single-argument binary width: INT(8) ... UINT(256)). So a `full` holding a comma misses whether or not the collapse ran.

At :256, truncateParenthetical returns s[:i] for i = index of the first '('. The collapse only rewrites `inner`, which lies strictly after that first '(' — head is built from s[:open] and is untouched. So the truncated key is byte-identical either way. This holds even for nested parentheticals, where `inner` itself contains a '(': the first '(' of the result still sits at len(head).

Therefore the two lines cannot change normaliseType's output for any input at all. This is dead code, not untested code, and no end-to-end fixture can ever pin it.

## Do not delete it

The lines become load-bearing the moment a comma-bearing row exists, and gqlc-5md (length/precision/scale field on PropertyType) is precisely the bead that adds one — DECIMAL(10,2) would start hitting :253, and a DECIMAL(10, 2) spelling that had not been collapsed would miss the new row and silently fall back to bare DECIMAL. That is the failure gqlc-5md's implementer would have to debug, having never seen this note.

## Proposed fix — pin the equivalence, not the key

Assert directly on canonicalSpelling that comma spacing does not change the lookup key:

    canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10, 2)") == canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10,2)")
    canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10 , 2)") == canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10,2)")

Asserting the equivalence rather than the literal string keeps the test tolerant of a future re-spelling of the canonical form, and it stays green after gqlc-5md lands rather than going red like gqlc-h9n.21 deliberately does. Testing the unexported helper directly has precedent: typeSpellingsRowFor (propertytype_test.go:440) already calls canonicalSpelling and truncateParenthetical.

## Also

collapseParenthetical's doc comment (propertytype.go:273-276) offers `FLOAT(10, 2)` as a motivating example of two spellings sharing a lookup key. They do share one — but that shared key is not a row, so the sharing buys nothing today. The comment should say which half of its claim is currently inert, the same comments-are-claims-not-facts problem found at resolve.go:66 in gqlc-zm2.

## Sweep survivors deliberately NOT filed

The other five survivors are all provably unable to change output and want no fixture:

  :279 / :283  the unbalanced-paren early returns. The grammar's LEFT_PAREN ... RIGHT_PAREN arms are always balanced, so neither branch is reachable; the :279 mutant is additionally masked by the :283 guard.
  :292         `+ s[end+1:]`. notNull is the only grammar element that can follow ')' (GQL.g4:1755, :1761, :1832, :1846, :1889), and canonicalSpelling:269 strips it one line before the collapse runs, so the tail is always empty.
  :297         TrimRight on the truncated head. collapseParenthetical:287 already trimmed that space before truncateParenthetical ever sees the string.
  :296         i >= 0 vs i > 0. No value-type spelling begins with '('.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: inferUnlabelled's multi-round loop is uncovered production code
description:
TRIPWIRE-L, planted during the gqlc-oou inference sweep (2026-07-28), put a panic at the top of the SECOND iteration of inferUnlabelled's outer 'for len(pending) > 0' loop. It never fired across go test ./... . No fixture in the resolver corpus needs more than one inference round.

This is NOT a fail-open defect and NOT provably unreachable -- it is genuinely uncovered production code. The corresponding mutation ('inference stops iterating past the first round', which caps the loop at one pass) SURVIVED the sweep for exactly this reason.

WHAT A FIXTURE WOULD NEED: a binding that is ambiguous when it is first evaluated but becomes unambiguous once a LATER binding in the same round commits its type. That requires a purpose-built schema -- none of social.gql / social_r2 / social_r5 / social_r6 / social_r7 / social_edgeunion has the right shape, because in all of them each unlabelled binding either resolves on its first look or never resolves at all.

Sketch of the shape needed: two unlabelled bindings b1 and b2 joined by an edge, where b1's candidate set is narrowed only by b2's committed type, and b2 is itself only resolvable after some third labelled anchor. Ordering matters -- the fixture must present b1 BEFORE b2 in whatever order inferUnlabelled walks pending, or the multi-round path is skipped again.

Until such a schema exists, the loop's termination behaviour, the carry-wins skip on already-carried bindings, and any interaction between rounds are all unexercised. Low priority: the single-round path is well pinned (25/37 caught in that sweep), and no known query shape reaches the second round.

Filed from gqlc-oou / PR #553.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: two pieces of dead code in scope.go — the Has* trio has no production callers, and virtualProjection's TypeList/TypeEdge stamp is never read
description:
Fell out of the gqlc-76y mutation sweep. Both are unreachable-by-construction, so
mutation testing can never cover them and no fixture would help. They need a
delete-or-keep decision instead.

## 1. scope.HasNode / HasEdge / HasCall have zero production callers

    grep -rn "\.HasNode(\|\.HasEdge(\|\.HasCall(" internal/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test.go
    -> nothing

They are only called from scope_test.go, as assertions about scope contents. The
HasEdge assertions there are all negative (require.False), which is why deleting an
arm of HasEdge leaves the suite green.

Options: delete them and have scope_test.go read the maps directly, or keep them as
deliberate test affordances and accept that they are uncovered by construction. If
kept, a comment saying so would stop the next sweep re-flagging them.

## 2. virtualProjection's variable-length arm is inert

scope.go:603-608 stamps query.TypeList{} on a wildcard-expanded RefProjection when
the edge binding is variable-length, and query.TypeEdge{} otherwise. That stamp is
never read:

- projectionType routes query.RefProjection to refProjectionType(pp.Ref(), sch),
  discarding pp.Type(). refProjectionType re-derives varLength from
  s.edgeBindings[...].Hops() itself (scope.go:682) and builds the ResolvedList there.
- Nothing downstream of the resolver reads it either. The only readers of
  query.TypeList are internal/query/cypher/typing.go and expr.go, both in the parser,
  which runs before the resolver; and resolve.go's resolveType, which RefProjection
  never reaches.

Proven rather than argued: collapsing the branch to always stamp TypeEdge survives
the full `go test ./...` on the gqlc-76y branch, where
valid/returns_all_var_length_edge.cypher's golden pins r as a list of edges. If the
stamp were observable that golden would have moved.

Options: delete the branch and always stamp TypeEdge (or TypeUnknown, since no value
is meaningful), or keep it as documentation of intent with a comment saying the
resolved type comes from refProjectionType.

Deliberately not doing either autonomously — these are production deletions and the
code may be scaffolding for a later stage.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Extended by a 33-mutation sweep of scope.go's projection lane (buildScopeOrder, materialiseReturns, virtualProjection, projectionType, refProjectionType, ResolveProjections), run 2026-07-28 at 9e743a3. 25/33 caught, no BUILD-FAILs.

THE STAMP FINDING IS WIDER THAN THIS BEAD RECORDS. gqlc-2y7 says virtualProjection's TypeList/TypeEdge stamp is never read. The sweep confirms that and adds the third:

    virtualProjection stamps a wildcard node as unknown        SURVIVED
    virtualProjection stops distinguishing a var-length edge   SURVIVED

The first replaces query.TypeNode{} with query.TypeUnknown{} in the node arm; nothing observes it. So ALL THREE of virtualProjection's Projection type stamps are inert, not just the edge pair — projectionType routes a RefProjection to refProjectionType, which re-derives the type from the binding tables and never consults the stamp it was handed. Whatever this bead does about the edge stamps should do the same for the node one, or the asymmetry becomes the next survivor.

NO NEW FAIL-OPENS IN THE PROJECTION LANE. The other six survivors were each probed or tripwired and are not test gaps, which is worth recording so the lane is not re-swept from scratch:

- buildScopeOrder's `v == "" || seen[v]` guard -- EQUIVALENT MUTANT, and this overturned my first reading. I expected removing it to let a re-referenced name into scopeOrder twice and emit a duplicate RETURN * column. It does not: the cypher parser's mergeBinding folds a re-reference into one binding record, so seen[v] never fires for a name in the tables, and an anonymous binding (v == "") is filtered by the three lookups below it anyway. Proven with a tripwire that panics when the guard fires AND the name would have passed a lookup: never fired across the whole suite.
- materialiseReturns' empty-scopeOrder short-circuit -- tripwire never fired; returnsAll with an empty scope is unreached.
- virtualProjection's out-of-scope error -- tripwire never fired. Documented in situ as a resolver-side-bug tripwire.
- projectionType's unknown-variant default -- defensive tripwire over a closed variant set.
- refProjectionType's final ErrOutOfR0Scope return -- tripwire never fired.
- the carried-alias bypass's `ref.Property == ""` condition -- documented unreachable in situ: the parser scope check rejects Ref{"c", "p"} unless c is a binding name in scope.

Sweep artefacts: /tmp/mkproj.py, /tmp/proj_cases.json, /tmp/proj_sweep.py.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Mutation-sweep evidence (from gqlc-l7v):

1. virtualProjection's TypeList stamp is now CONFIRMED unread, not
   suspected. The mutation 'a wildcard var-length edge stops projecting
   as a list' — deleting the TypeList wrapper entirely — SURVIVED the
   full suite. Nothing downstream consumes it.

2. New instance in the same family: callBindingSlot (resolve.go:104)
   declares resultType, nullable, procedure and sourceField. Only
   resultType is ever read (scope.go:612, resolve.go:724). The other
   three are write-only.

3. Third instance: buildScopeOrder's local-loop '|| seen[v]' dedup is
   unreachable. TRIPWIRE-S (panic on a duplicate name arriving in the
   local loop) never fired across the whole suite — the cypher parser
   already dedups binding records before the resolver sees them.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
callBindingSlot's write-only fields, now proven by deletion rather than by grep
(follow-up to the 13:36 comment's finding 2, arriving from gqlc-bef item 5).

Deleting a field together with its write at scope.go:230-235 and rebuilding is a
sharper instrument than grepping for readers, because it also catches reads
through struct literals, embedding and reflection. Measured one field at a time
and all three together:

    nullable only      UNREAD    go build ./... = 0, go vet = 0, go test ./internal/... = 0
    sourceField only   UNREAD    go build ./... = 0, go vet = 0, go test ./internal/... = 0
    procedure only     build ./... = 0, TEST BUILD FAILS
    all three          build ./... = 0, TEST BUILD FAILS

So the 13:36 claim holds, with one correction worth writing down: `procedure`
has no reader either. It appears exactly once outside the write, at
scope_test.go:140, as a field NAME in the struct literal
`map[string]callBindingSlot{"c": {procedure: "test.proc"}}` — a value the test
constructs and never reads back. That is a construction reference, not a read,
but it does mean deleting `procedure` is a two-file change while deleting
`nullable` or `sourceField` is a one-file change.

The full reader set for the struct is two sites, both on resultType:

    grep -rn "\.procedure\|\.sourceField\|\.resultType" internal/resolver/
    resolve.go:724   switch slot.resultType.(type) {
    scope.go:612     return query.NewRefProjection(query.Ref{Variable: name}, slot.resultType), nil

WHY THE nullable FIELD IS THE INTERESTING ONE. gqlc-bef filed it as a test gap —
"no fixture yields a nullable CALL YIELD scalar, so the bit could be hard-wired
false". Both halves of that were wrong. A fixture does exist
(valid/call_standalone_yield_star_string_nullable.cypher, whose golden pins
"nullable": true), and the bit survives being hard-wired in EITHER direction:

    nullable: false   SURVIVED
    nullable: true    SURVIVED

A mutation surviving in both directions is the signature of a dead write, and it
is worth treating as a distinct sweep verdict — a live field can survive being
pinned to its common value, but it cannot survive being pinned to the wrong one.
Projection nullability reaches the golden by a different lane entirely:
callProjectionType (resolve.go:719-722) reads nullableBinding[ref.Variable].

The doc comment at resolve.go:104-106 is what made this look load-bearing — it
says the slot carries "bridged Stage-6 type, nullability, and the two identity
strings codegen may consult on the query.Query side (spec §4.1)". Codegen never
sees them: exportedCallTypes is resolver-internal, and scope.go:866 says so
outright ("carry-only lanes and callTypes are NOT observable through..."). If
the delete-or-keep decision lands on keep, that comment is the thing to fix,
because it is the reason two separate sweeps have now flagged these fields.

Still not deleting anything autonomously — same posture as the rest of this bead.

title: schema/gql: nothing pins that a syntax error names the offending token
description:
listener.SyntaxError has two branches, and the interesting one is unasserted. Deleting it -- so every syntax error falls through to the bare \"syntax error at %d:%d: %s\" form and never names the offending token -- passes the whole suite.

Measured at 61a6cd1 as part of a 19-mutation sweep of listener.go; 17 were caught and this was one of the two that were not.

listener.go states the reason for the branch: \"Naming the offending token alongside line:column makes the location concrete for a schema author scanning their source.\" Two places could have pinned it and neither does:

  invalidFixtures maps syntax_error.gql to nil, which TestInvalid documents as \"any non-nil error from the syntax error listener satisfies it\" -- so the message is not read at all.
  TestPropertyBareDurationRejectedAtParse asserts strings.HasPrefix(err.Error(), \"syntax error at \"), which is the half both branches share.
